narrativeReportMd:
# TerminologyCapabilities R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`TerminologyCapabilities` keeps its identity in R6, but local content-model changes create real migration breaks. The highest-impact issues are removal of `closure`, replacement of the required `codeSearch` code system, the new required `codeSystem.content` child, and new error constraints that reject duplicate code-system/version declarations.

## Scope
The analysis is limited to the local `TerminologyCapabilities` StructureDefinition and directly bound local terminology artifacts. Inherited base-resource changes are out of scope and should be handled by the relevant base-artifact reports.

## Main migration themes
R4 instances that describe terminology-server details need active normalization before R6 validation: map or review `codeSearch`, populate `codeSystem.content` whenever `codeSystem` is present, consolidate duplicate code-system/version entries, and remove or transform `closure`. R6 instances also gain several expressivity features, especially CodeSystem supplement support, that cannot be represented in R4 without extensions or loss.

## Highest-impact findings
High-risk findings are `TerminologyCapabilities:TERMINOLOGY_BINDING:TerminologyCapabilities.codeSearch:4f18c2`, `TerminologyCapabilities:CARDINALITY:TerminologyCapabilities.codeSystem.content:8d71a5`, and `TerminologyCapabilities:VALUE_CONSTRAINT:TerminologyCapabilities.codeSystem:17b6aa`.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for `codeSearch` semantic mapping, choosing `codeSystem.content`, interpreting arbitrary language codes against the R6 language binding, and deciding whether R6 supplement-support declarations can be safely dropped when converting to R4.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several changes could have been made less disruptive by preserving old optional elements or old terminology codes with deprecation guidance. The stricter R6 model appears aimed at making terminology capability declarations more precise and less ambiguous, but conversion is not purely mechanical for all instances.

## Follow-up analysis
Separate analysis of the `$closure` operation, CodeSystem supplement terminology support, and the base Resource/DomainResource reports would improve migration planning.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `TerminologyCapabilities` has material local breaking changes despite stable artifact identity. The top migration concerns are the `codeSearch` code-system replacement, mandatory `codeSystem.content`, stricter code-system uniqueness/default constraints, and removal of `closure`. The main uncertainty is semantic mapping for old `codeSearch` and `$closure` behavior without official diff notes or operation narrative.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should validate old instances against the new R6 constraints rather than relying on structural name matching. Systems need a policy for removed `closure`, a manual or rules-based mapping for `codeSearch`, a way to populate `codeSystem.content`, deduplication of `codeSystem` entries and version defaults, and extensions or loss annotations for R6-only supplement and canonical-resource metadata when down-converting to R4.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural and binding deltas because both core StructureDefinitions and the local CodeSystems/ValueSets were available. Confidence is lower for semantic intent and best mappings because no official diff, JIRA rationale, narrative pages, or ConceptMaps were available locally.

findings.title: R6 removes the TerminologyCapabilities.closure subtree

oldState.summary: R4 had optional `closure` support details with optional `closure.translation`.
oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 instance could advertise support for the ConceptMap `$closure` operation using `TerminologyCapabilities.closure`, and could state cross-system closure support using `closure.translation`.

newState.narrativeMd: The R6 local StructureDefinition contains no `closure` element or replacement child under `TerminologyCapabilities`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R4 element id is absent from the R6 snapshot and differential. No same-parent R6 element with equivalent closure semantics appears in the R6 TerminologyCapabilities definition.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation and parsing break for any R4 instance that includes `closure`: R6 validators and generated models will treat the element as unknown because it is no longer in the resource content model.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is primarily capability-discovery loss for terminology clients that rely on advertised `$closure` support, not direct patient safety.

justification.inferredGoal: Remove or relocate `$closure` capability advertising from TerminologyCapabilities.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `closure` as an optional deprecated legacy element for one release.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The removal appears aimed at dropping `$closure` capability advertising from the base resource; the R6 package has no matching `closure` element and no local closure OperationDefinition. That goal is reasonable, but the evidence does not prove that immediate invalidation of legacy declarations was the only viable path.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep `TerminologyCapabilities.closure` 0..1, mark it deprecated or legacy, and direct R6 systems to the replacement capability mechanism if one exists. This would accept R4 instances, but it would also leave R6 clients seeing a capability for an operation no longer represented in the R6 package, so the alternative is only partial.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old instances but keeps an operation-specific capability hook after the R6 package no longer defines the closure operation.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `TerminologyCapabilities.closure` as 0..1 BackboneElement.
R4 defines `closure.translation` as optional boolean.
No R6 element id begins with `TerminologyCapabilities.closure`.

examples.examplesMd: The example is intentionally minimal and shows an R4-supported `closure` declaration that has no R6 element to receive it.

findings.narrativeMd: `TerminologyCapabilities.closure` disappeared from the local R6 resource model. Existing R4 capability statements that advertise `$closure` behavior with this element will fail strict R6 validation and will also break generated R6 model classes that have no closure property.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid instance containing `closure` becomes R6-invalid because the element is unknown. This finding is not an R6-to-R4 problem because R6 has no corresponding element to back-port.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Before R6 validation, remove `closure` or transform it to a site-specific extension or other documented capability mechanism. Migration tests should include an R4 instance with `closure.translation` to ensure the transform does not silently discard an operational capability that clients still depend on.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The backward-compatible alternative was to retain the optional element with a deprecation note. Without official rationale, the removal appears disruptive for the small set of systems that used `$closure` capability discovery.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm against the R6 `$closure` OperationDefinition or terminology narrative before deciding whether the capability can be dropped.

findings.title: codeSearch required codes were replaced

oldState.summary: R4 `codeSearch` was bound required to `code-search-support|4.0.1` with codes `explicit` and `all`.

binding.description: The degree to which the server supports the code search parameter on ValueSet, if it is supported.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: Local CodeSystem definitions, not live terminology expansion, were compared.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 distinguished support for searching explicitly detailed codes versus all codes based on expansion.

newState.summary: R6 `codeSearch` is required-bound to `code-search-support|6.0.0-ballot4` with `in-compose`, `in-expansion`, and `in-compose-or-expansion`.

binding.description: The degree to which the server supports the code search parameter on ValueSet, if it is supported.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R6 CodeSystem changes both code literals and definitions, so exact automated mapping is not guaranteed.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 expresses whether ValueSet `code` search is against compose, expansion, or both.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element path and type are unchanged, but the required value set's code system content was replaced.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Because the binding is required in both releases, R4 instances using `explicit` or `all` are invalid in R6, and R6 instances using any new code are invalid in R4. Generated enums, switch statements, persistence constraints, and UI labels must change.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect mapping can cause clients to overestimate or underestimate a server's ValueSet code-search behavior.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify whether ValueSet code search operates over compose, expansion, or both.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `explicit` and `all` as deprecated codes while adding the R6 compose/expansion codes.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 codes express a more precise compose-versus-expansion model for ValueSet code search, and the old `explicit`/`all` split does not have a clear one-to-one mapping. Replacing a required code system is disruptive, but the cleaner model is probably reasonable because retaining the old literals would weaken the precision of the base R6 declaration.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would include `explicit` and `all` in the R6 required value set as deprecated aliases, alongside `in-compose`, `in-expansion`, and `in-compose-or-expansion`. That would preserve R4 instances, but it would keep two generations of search semantics in the same enum and require clients to support unclear legacy meanings indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves validation compatibility but forces R6 clients to handle ambiguous legacy enum semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 binding is required to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/code-search-support|4.0.1`.
R4 code system contains `explicit` and `all`.
R6 binding is required to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/code-search-support|6.0.0-ballot4`.
R6 code system contains `in-compose`, `in-expansion`, and `in-compose-or-expansion`.

examples.examplesMd: The fragments are minimal but illustrate the required-binding incompatibility in both directions.

findings.narrativeMd: `TerminologyCapabilities.codeSearch` kept the same path but changed its required code system. This is a classic enum break: old code literals no longer validate, new code literals cannot be represented in R4, and old code handling logic will miss the R6 values.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `codeSearch: explicit` or `codeSearch: all` are old-valid/new-invalid. R6 instances using `in-compose`, `in-expansion`, or `in-compose-or-expansion` are not cleanly R4-representable without an extension or lossy mapping.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not blindly rename codes. Review server behavior and map `all` and `explicit` to the R6 compose/expansion model using local policy or a ConceptMap if one becomes available. Update generated enums, tests, UI text, validation fixtures, and database constraints.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The new model is probably clearer, but replacing a required code system is highly disruptive. A transitional required value set containing both old and new codes, plus deprecation metadata, would have been more compatible.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: No local ConceptMap was found. Mapping `explicit` is especially ambiguous because the R4 definition mentions codes explicitly detailed on includes or expansions.

findings.title: Each R6 codeSystem entry must now declare content mode

oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 `codeSystem` entry could consist only of a URI, versions, filters, properties, or subsumption details.

newState.summary: R6 adds `codeSystem.content` with cardinality 1..1 and required binding to CodeSystemContentMode.

binding.description: The extent of the content of the code system (the concepts and codes it defines) are represented in a code system resource.

newState.narrativeMd: Whenever an R6 instance includes `codeSystem`, it must say how much of the code system content is represented.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element has no R4 counterpart under `TerminologyCapabilities.codeSystem`; it appears as a new required child in R6.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any R4 instance with at least one `codeSystem` entry and no `content` value is invalid in R6. Conversely, the R6 content-mode assertion has no native R4 location and is lost unless preserved in an extension.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrectly inferred content mode can mislead clients about whether a terminology server exposes complete, fragmentary, or supplement code-system content.

justification.inferredGoal: Make each advertised code system explicit about the extent of available content.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `codeSystem.content` as optional first, with a warning or best-practice invariant.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Requiring content mode makes each advertised code system clearer for clients and aligns TerminologyCapabilities with CodeSystem content-mode semantics. The breakage is material because old `codeSystem` entries cannot supply the value, but an optional-first approach would not meet the R6 goal of making the base declaration unambiguous.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The less-breaking base design would define `TerminologyCapabilities.codeSystem.content` as 0..1 in R6 and add conformance text or a warning recommending it. That preserves R4 instances, but base R6 validators would still accept incomplete code-system capability declarations, so the alternative is only partial.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old `codeSystem` entries but leaves base R6 declarations allowed to omit an important content-mode assertion.

evidence.detail: R4 has no `TerminologyCapabilities.codeSystem.content` element.
R6 defines `codeSystem.content` as 1..1 code with required binding.
R6 allowed content-mode codes are `not-present`, `example`, `fragment`, `complete`, and `supplement`.
The R6 terminology-server example populates `content: complete` on codeSystem entries.

examples.examplesMd: The R4 fragment omits `content`, which was impossible to provide natively in R4. The R6 fragment contains information that cannot be represented natively in R4.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds a mandatory `content` code inside each `codeSystem` entry. This is not just an optional R6 enhancement: it makes old code-system declarations incomplete unless a migration can determine whether the server provides complete, fragmentary, example, no-present, or supplement content.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances that include `codeSystem` but omit `codeSystem.content` become invalid in R6. Valid R6 content-mode data is not natively representable in R4.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all R4 instances with `codeSystem`. For each entry, populate `content` from authoritative server knowledge rather than guessing. If the value cannot be determined, use a migration exception workflow or profile-specific policy and test all five R6 content-mode codes.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The stricter requirement is useful for interoperability, but it could have been introduced as optional first. Making it mandatory in the base resource forces semantic decisions during migration.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The R6 binding URL is versioned `|6.0.0` in the R6 ballot StructureDefinition, not `|6.0.0-ballot4`.

findings.title: R6 adds error constraints requiring distinct code-system and version declarations

oldState.summary: R4 only enforced that multiple versions have version codes.

constraints.human: If there is more than one version, a version code must be defined

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 did not prohibit multiple `codeSystem` repetitions with the same URI, duplicate `version.code` values, or multiple default versions.

newState.summary: R6 keeps tcp-1 and adds tcp-6, tcp-7, and tcp-8 as error constraints.

constraints.human: Each instance of the codeSystem element must represent a distinct code system.
Each version.code element must be distinct for a particular code system.
A codeSystem element instance may have at most one version.isDefault element with a value of 'true'.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 requires unique code-system URI entries, unique version codes within a code system, and no more than one default version.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The constraints are on the same local root/codeSystem element family and appear in the R6 StructureDefinition only.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The new constraints have severity `error`. R4 instances that used repeated `codeSystem` entries for the same URI, repeated version codes, or more than one default version can be structurally valid in R4 but fail R6 validation.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Ambiguous defaults can cause clients to choose the wrong terminology version; the migration risk is mostly operational correctness.

justification.inferredGoal: Eliminate ambiguous code-system declarations and default-version conflicts.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Introduce tcp-6, tcp-7, and tcp-8 as warning-level constraints before error-level enforcement.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The new constraints remove ambiguous duplicate code-system URIs, duplicate version codes, and multiple default versions. Because those patterns directly affect how clients interpret a terminology server's supported systems and defaults, warning-only compatibility would not satisfy the base R6 goal. The breaking design is still proportionate because affected legacy instances can generally be normalized by merging duplicates and choosing one default.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would add the same invariants as warnings in R6 and convert them to errors later. That would preserve old instances, but it would knowingly allow contradictory base R6 capability statements, so it is a partial alternative with a material interoperability tradeoff.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Warnings ease migration but do not give clients reliable uniqueness and default-version semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 has tcp-1 but not tcp-6, tcp-7, or tcp-8.
R6 adds an error rule requiring distinct `codeSystem.uri` values.
R6 adds error rules for distinct version codes and at most one default version.

examples.examplesMd: The example illustrates duplicate `codeSystem.uri` and duplicate defaults. In R6 it would also need `codeSystem.content`; the uniqueness constraints are the material point of this finding.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 turns several implicit data-quality expectations into validator-enforced rules. Implementations that modeled each version or server facet as a separate `codeSystem` repetition can no longer do so if the URI repeats.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is old-valid/new-invalid whenever the duplicate patterns occur. It does not create a new R6-to-R4 representability problem because R4 is looser.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Group code-system declarations by URI, merge duplicate versions, ensure `version.code` is unique within each grouped entry, and choose a single `isDefault=true` version. Add tests for duplicate URI, duplicate version code, two defaults, and absent default.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The constraints are likely justified because duplicate declarations are ambiguous. However, imposing them as base errors rather than warnings creates immediate validation failures for legacy data.

findings.title: codeSystem.version.language now has a required all-languages binding

oldState.summary: R4 had a repeating `code` element for supported display languages with no local binding.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed any lexical FHIR `code` value for `codeSystem.version.language`.

newState.summary: R6 keeps the same cardinality and type but adds a required binding to `all-languages|6.0.0-ballot4`.

binding.description: IETF language tag for a human language

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: No full expansion was computed; the material change is the addition of a required binding where R4 had none.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 language declarations must be valid members of the all-languages value set, with common languages as an additional starter binding.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element path and type are unchanged; the material delta is the new required terminology binding.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using non-language or private language tokens could validate structurally in R4 but fail required-binding validation in R6. R6-to-R4 representability is low risk because R4 can carry the code, though it will not enforce the same semantics.

justification.inferredGoal: Ensure language support declarations use valid IETF language tags.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Use an extensible or preferred all-languages binding before making it required.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The element represents supported display languages, so requiring valid language tags is a reasonable conformance improvement. The alternative is real but incomplete: it would reduce validation failures for private or malformed R4 tokens while continuing to permit values that do not satisfy the element's semantics.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would bind `codeSystem.version.language` to all-languages with extensible or preferred strength, or add a warning invariant first. That preserves more R4 instances, but it does not give R6 clients a dependable guarantee that repeated values are language tags.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: A weaker binding preserves nonstandard legacy tokens but does not ensure language declarations are valid language tags.

evidence.detail: R4 element has type `code` and no binding.
R6 adds required binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/all-languages|6.0.0-ballot4`.

examples.examplesMd: The example focuses on the language code. It is illustrative; a migrated R6 instance would also need `codeSystem.content`.

findings.narrativeMd: The local display-language declaration changed from an unconstrained code to a required language-tag binding. This is a validation improvement but can break instances that used local tokens or non-standard language identifiers.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: The break is potential because conformant real-world R4 instances likely used language tags already. Invalid or private tokens accepted by R4's unconstrained code type can become R6-invalid.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Normalize values to valid IETF language tags before R6 validation. Keep a reject list for non-language tokens and decide whether private-use tags are acceptable under the R6 value set expansion used by your validator.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The strengthened binding is justified by the element's meaning. A preferred or extensible transitional binding would have reduced validation failures but allowed poor-quality data.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: A terminology server expansion of `all-languages` would improve confidence for edge cases such as private-use or grandfathered BCP 47 tags.

findings.title: Two local string fields changed to markdown

oldState.narrativeMd: Both fields serialized as JSON strings in R4 and were usually handled by generated string properties.

newState.narrativeMd: The JSON primitive representation remains a string, but the FHIR type name and rendering semantics changed.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element paths are unchanged and only their primitive type names changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Most existing JSON values remain lexically compatible, but generated models, type-specific validation, UI rendering, and documentation sanitization can change. R6 markdown can be stored in an R4 string but R4 consumers may not render or sanitize it as markdown.

justification.inferredGoal: Permit richer formatted descriptions and parameter documentation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the primitive type as `string` and state in definitions that Markdown content is allowed or expected.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The serialized JSON values remain strings, so this is mainly a code generation and rendering break rather than an instance-validation break. Using the `markdown` primitive is still probably reasonable for descriptive fields because it gives tools a computable signal for formatting and sanitization.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would retain the R4 `string` type and update comments to permit Markdown conventions. That would preserve generated string properties, but it would not let validators, renderers, or security filters identify Markdown-bearing fields from the type system, so it is only a partial alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids codegen churn but leaves rendering and sanitization semantics non-computable.

evidence.detail: R4 type is `string`.
R6 type is `markdown`.
R4 type is `string`.
R6 type is `markdown`.

examples.examplesMd: The serialized JSON property names do not change; the migration concern is generated type and rendering behavior.

findings.narrativeMd: Two local descriptive fields now carry the FHIR `markdown` primitive type instead of `string`. This is unlikely to invalidate ordinary JSON instances but can break strict code generators and consumers that attach type-specific behavior to primitive types.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is mostly a runtime/codegen risk rather than a hard instance break. R6 markdown values are JSON strings and can be placed into R4 string fields, but markdown semantics and sanitization may be lost.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Regenerate models and update serializers, validators, and UI rendering paths for these two fields. Tests should include plain text, markdown formatting, and any local sanitization rules.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible option was to keep `string` and use comments to permit markdown conventions. The R6 change is more strongly typed but creates generated-code churn.

findings.title: R6 adds optional canonical metadata fields that R4 cannot natively represent

oldState.summary: R4 did not have `identifier`, `versionAlgorithm[x]`, or `copyrightLabel` on TerminologyCapabilities.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 instances could carry the canonical URL, version, copyright, and other metadata, but not these three fields natively.

newState.narrativeMd: These fields support richer canonical-resource metadata and version comparison behavior.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The elements are present in the R6 local snapshot and absent from the R4 local snapshot.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4-to-R6 validation is not harmed because the fields are optional additions. R6-to-R4 conversion is lossy unless these fields are dropped or represented with extensions.

justification.inferredGoal: Align TerminologyCapabilities with richer canonical-resource metadata patterns.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking base R6 alternative is needed because these are optional R6 additions that preserve R4 instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding optional `identifier`, `versionAlgorithm[x]`, and `copyrightLabel` improves canonical-resource metadata without making any R4 instance invalid in R6. The reported risk is R6-to-R4 loss, not R4-to-R6 base-design breakage.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Using extensions can help preserve these fields when converting R6 content back to R4, but extension/backport support is not a backward-compatible base R6 design alternative. For R4-to-R6 compatibility, the optional additions are already non-breaking.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R4 extensions can reduce down-conversion loss, but that is a round-trip mitigation rather than a base R4-to-R6 alternative.

evidence.detail: R6 adds `identifier` 0..* Identifier.
R6 adds `versionAlgorithm[x]` with string and Coding choices.
R6 adds `copyrightLabel` 0..1 string.
No corresponding R4 elements exist.

examples.examplesMd: R4 has no native properties for these R6 elements; an extension strategy is needed to preserve them.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds several optional metadata properties that make TerminologyCapabilities more expressive but create down-conversion loss. The R6 examples already use `identifier`.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Existing R4 instances remain valid with respect to these additions. Valid R6 instances using these fields are not cleanly R4-representable without extensions.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4, decide whether to drop the fields, map them to standard or custom extensions, or preserve them in an out-of-band migration envelope. Pay special attention to `versionAlgorithm[x]` because losing it can affect version ordering.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding optional elements is the least disruptive way to improve R6 expressivity, but not representable in R4. Extensions would be more backward-compatible but less convenient for R6 implementers.

findings.title: R6 adds CodeSystem supplement capability declarations that R4 cannot natively represent

oldState.summary: R4 had no native `supplements` backbone and no `codeSystem.supplement` or `codeSystem.version.supplement` declarations.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 TerminologyCapabilities could describe code systems and versions but could not explicitly advertise CodeSystem supplement or global language-pack support.

newState.summary: R6 adds supplement references under code systems and a root `supplements` backbone with `globals`.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 can describe supported supplements for all versions, supplements for a particular code-system version, and global language-pack support.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: All supplement-related elements are new in the R6 local snapshot with no R4 counterpart.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These optional additions do not invalidate R4 instances during R4-to-R6 migration, but they carry terminology capability semantics that R4 cannot represent natively. Dropping them can cause R4 clients to miss supplement and language-pack behavior.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Loss of supplement support declarations can affect terminology display, designation, and property behavior.

justification.inferredGoal: Expose CodeSystem supplement and global language-pack support in terminology server capability statements.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking base R6 alternative is needed because the supplement-support elements are optional R6 additions.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 supplement and global language-pack fields add terminology capability expressivity without invalidating R4 instances. The incompatibility is that R4 cannot natively represent the new R6 information, which is a down-conversion and round-trip concern rather than a base R4-to-R6 break.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A cross-version extension strategy could be useful for R4 clients that must understand supplement support, but that is a mitigation for R6-to-R4 representation loss. It should not be counted as a `Yes` or `Partial` base-design alternative for R4-to-R6 compatibility.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R4 extensions may preserve supplement semantics during down-conversion, but they are not needed to protect R4-to-R6 validation.

evidence.detail: R6 adds a code-system-level supplement canonical reference.
R6 adds a version-level supplement canonical reference.
R6 adds `supplements.globals` bound required to the Global LangPack Support value set.
R6 global langpack support codes are `not-supported`, `explicit`, and `implicit`.

examples.examplesMd: R4 has no native supplement-support fields, so this R6 capability information requires extensions or must be dropped.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 introduces a new supplement-support model for terminology capabilities. This is not an R4-to-R6 validation break, but it is a significant R6-to-R4 semantic loss risk for systems that need to advertise language packs, designations, or other CodeSystem supplement behavior.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 validators will reject these R6 elements as unknown. If the elements are dropped, the R4 representation remains syntactically valid but no longer communicates the supplement capability.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Define a cross-version extension strategy if R4 clients must understand supplement support. Otherwise document the loss during R6-to-R4 conversion and avoid treating the R4 result as a faithful capability statement for terminology displays or designations.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Native R6 elements are understandable for new clients but not backward-compatible with R4. A published extension could bridge both versions at the cost of weaker native support.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Assess alongside CodeSystem supplement and designation behavior in the broader terminology package.

findings.title: jurisdiction semantics changed and R6 recommends useContext for jurisdiction

oldState.summary: R4 described jurisdiction as the intended jurisdiction for the terminology capabilities.

semanticText.short: Intended jurisdiction for terminology capabilities (if applicable)
semanticText.definition: A legal or geographic region in which the terminology capabilities is intended to be used.

newState.summary: R6 describes jurisdiction as the authority's jurisdiction and includes a deprecation note encouraging useContext jurisdiction.

semanticText.short: Jurisdiction of the authority that maintains the terminology capabilities (if applicable)
semanticText.definition: A legal or geographic region in which the authority that maintains the resource is operating.
semanticText.comment: Implementations are encouraged to migrate to using the new jurisdiction code in the useContext element.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same element path remains, but definition/comment and canonical value set URL changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Cardinality, type, and binding strength did not tighten. The risk is semantic: data that meant intended-use jurisdiction in R4 may be interpreted as maintaining-authority jurisdiction in R6.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify jurisdiction semantics and move intended-use jurisdiction into useContext.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 intended-use meaning and add a separate authority-jurisdiction representation.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: R6 consistently shifts canonical-resource `jurisdiction` text toward the maintaining authority and points intended-use jurisdiction to `useContext`, so the goal is reasonable. The semantic reinterpretation can still surprise systems carrying R4 intended-use values; the less-breaking alternative has material model-consistency and duplicate-representation costs.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have left `TerminologyCapabilities.jurisdiction` with its R4 intended-use meaning and added a new authority-jurisdiction element or explicit useContext pattern for the maintaining authority. That would preserve old semantics, but it would make TerminologyCapabilities diverge from the broader R6 canonical-resource model and leave parallel places for jurisdiction facts, so the alternative is partial rather than clearly superior.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old semantics but duplicates jurisdiction concepts and conflicts with the broader R6 canonical-resource pattern.

evidence.detail: R4 definition says the jurisdiction where the terminology capabilities is intended to be used.
R6 definition says jurisdiction of the maintaining authority and adds a deprecation note recommending useContext jurisdiction.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example shows the R6-comment-recommended useContext pattern. Exact coding systems should follow project policy and terminology guidance.

findings.narrativeMd: The `jurisdiction` element did not become structurally invalid, but its R6 definition shifted from intended jurisdiction to maintaining-authority jurisdiction, with guidance to use `useContext` for jurisdictional use context. This can cause semantic reinterpretation during migration.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is not a hard validator break. Existing values remain structurally valid, but consumers may interpret the same data differently in R6.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review whether existing R4 `jurisdiction` values mean intended use or authority location. If they mean intended use, consider migrating them to `useContext` using the jurisdiction usage-context code while preserving authority jurisdiction separately if known.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The semantic change was avoidable by introducing a separate authority-jurisdiction concept or relying on comments only. Because the element name is unchanged, implementers need explicit data-governance review.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, abstract flag, derivation, and baseDefinition are unchanged. Maturity/status changed but does not create an identity split or rename.
All local additions/removals judged material are covered in findings. No renamed or moved local elements were detected beyond the removed `closure` subtree and added R6-only elements.
Common local elements kept the same min/max cardinalities. The material new required child `codeSystem.content` is reported separately.
No choice-type removals or reference-target narrowing were found. The material `string` to `markdown` replacements are reported separately.
`codeSystem.uri` remains canonical(CodeSystem). R6 adds supplement canonical(CodeSystem) references, which are covered as R6-to-R4 conversion risk.

`status` and `kind` remain required-bound with the same local code sets in the inspected CodeSystems. Material binding changes for `codeSearch`, `codeSystem.content`, `codeSystem.version.language`, and `supplements.globals` are covered.
No local modifier flag changed. `status` remains a modifier and no new local modifier element was introduced.

Common local summary flags are materially stable after treating absent `mustSupport` as false. New summary elements such as `identifier`, `versionAlgorithm[x]`, and `codeSystem.content` are covered as additions.
No local slicing or discriminator changes were found.
No local fixed values, pattern values, or default values were found to change materially.
No local maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue changes were identified beyond constraints and terminology bindings reported separately.
No local JSON property rename or choice-type removal was found. Serialization impact is from removed/added elements and primitive type name changes reported in findings.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Artifact maturity increased in R6
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The resource keeps the same identity and remains a concrete DomainResource specialization. The StructureDefinition status changes from `draft` to `active`, standards status from trial-use to normative, and FMM from 0 to 1, but instance shape does not break because of those metadata changes alone.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Organizations may treat normative/active status as a governance signal when prioritizing migration and conformance testing.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Name and URL warnings were updated
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 changes the name warning key/expression from `tcp-0` to `cnl-0` and adds warning `cnl-1` on `url`; both are warnings, not errors. They do not by themselves make instances invalid, though validators may surface new warnings.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: One-character names that satisfied the R4 warning expression may trigger the R6 warning, and canonical URLs containing `|`, `#`, or spaces should be cleaned up.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: PublicationStatus and CapabilityStatementKind bindings were version-updated without code-set change
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The binding URLs now point to R6 value-set versions, but the inspected local CodeSystems for `publication-status` and `capability-statement-kind` contain the same code literals as R4.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Generated enum package names or version metadata may change even though instance code values remain stable.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Several textual metadata fields are explicitly marked translatable in R6
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 adds translatable extensions to fields such as title, publisher, description, purpose, copyright, copyrightLabel, and implementation.description. These annotations do not invalidate R4 instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Localization tooling may begin treating these fields differently in R6.
